nameStory: The name "rapeseed" comes from the Latin word "rapum," meaning turnip, since this plant is closely related to turnips and has similar thick, fleshy roots. The "seed" part is obvious - this plant is grown primarily for its oil-rich seeds. You might know this plant better as "canola," which is actually a marketing-friendly name created from "CANadian Oil Low Acid" to describe varieties bred to be safe for human consumption.
description: Rapeseed is a tall, annual crop plant that can grow 3-5 feet high with bright yellow, four-petaled flowers clustered at the top of branching stems. It looks like a supersized version of wild mustard, with thick, blue-green leaves and a sturdy main stem. The plant produces long, narrow seed pods after flowering, packed with small, dark seeds that are pressed for oil. While primarily a farm crop, rapeseed occasionally escapes cultivation and can be found growing wild in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with exactly four petals arranged in a cross shape, clustered in dense groups at stem tips. Each flower is about half an inch across with a sweet, honey-like fragrance that attracts bees from far away.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are deeply lobed and feel slightly waxy or smooth to the touch, while upper leaves clasp the stem with ear-like projections. The blue-green color is distinctive and the leaves have a slightly bitter, cabbage-like smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright plant reaching 3-5 feet with a thick, sturdy main stem that branches near the top into multiple flower clusters. The whole plant has a robust, well-fed appearance compared to scraggly wild mustards.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, narrow seed pods (called siliques) that are 2-4 inches long and contain small, round, dark brown or black seeds. The pods make a rattling sound when shaken and split open with a satisfying pop when ripe.

habitat: Rapeseed is primarily found near agricultural areas, along roadsides adjacent to farm fields, and in disturbed soils where seeds have escaped from cultivation. In New England, it occasionally appears in abandoned lots, field edges, and waste places, particularly in areas with rich, well-drained soil.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate early and plants develop their rosette of lobed basal leaves. Young plants are low and leafy without the characteristic tall stem yet.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with masses of bright yellow flowers creating spectacular displays. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive four-petaled flowers are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and turn brown, eventually splitting open to release seeds. Plants begin to die back and become brown and brittle.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist, appearing as tall, dried stalks with remnants of split seed pods, though most plant material has decomposed by late winter.

funFact: A single rapeseed plant can produce up to 3,000 seeds, and those tiny seeds contain about 40% oil - that's such a high concentration that if you crushed a handful of seeds, you'd literally see oil droplets ooze out between your fingers!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with field mustard and other wild mustards, but rapeseed is much taller and more robust with thicker stems and larger flower clusters. Memory trick: "Rapeseed is the bodybuilder of the mustard family" - everything about it is bigger and beefier than its wild cousins.
contextualKnowledge: You might see this plant labeled as "canola" in agricultural contexts - they're the same species, but canola refers specifically to varieties bred to be low in erucic acid and safe for human consumption. The original rapeseed contained compounds that were mildly toxic, which is why the food-safe varieties got their own marketing name.
compareHints: Compared to field mustard, rapeseed is much taller and more robust with thicker stems and larger flower clusters. Unlike brown mustard, which has smaller, paler yellow flowers, rapeseed flowers are bright golden and more densely packed. It's also much more substantial-looking than the cabbage family vegetables, growing as a tall flowering plant rather than the compact heads we see in gardens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Field mustard is smaller and weedier-looking than its cultivated cousins like cabbage and broccoli, but shares their four-petaled yellow flowers (though cabbage family crops are usually harvested before flowering).
Unlike its relatives field mustard and brown mustard, wild cabbage has distinctively thick, waxy, blue-green leaves rather than thin, bright green ones.
Brown mustard differs from its close relative field mustard by having more deeply divided, darker leaves and a taller, more robust growth habit.
